title: Lab 5 – Hypercalcaemia, hypocalcaemia, osteoporosis
html:
Source: LP 5.pdf – 10 pages

Hypercalcemia- causes #1

  • Common Uncommon
  •  Hyperparathyroidism:  Vitamin D intoxication
  • primary, tertiary  Familial hypocalciuric
  •  Malignancy: hypercalcemia
  • – Multiple myeloma  Sarcoidosis and other
  • – Bony metastases granulomatous diseases
  • – PTH-related peptides  Thiazide diuretics
  • (paraneoplastic  Immobilization
  • syndromes-  Hyperthyroidism
  •  Renal failure
  • lung/GI/pancreatic
  • cancer)
  • Primary hyperparathyroidism
  • Caused by:
  •  A single parathyroid adenoma (80% of cases)
  •  Primary hyperplasia of the parathyroids (10–15% of cases)- more frequently
  • encountered in MEN 1 and MEN 2A syndromes *
  •  Parathyroid carcinoma (1–2% of cases)
  • *MEN type 1: primary hyperparathyroidism + pancreatic tumors + pituitary tumors (3Ps)
  • MEN type 2a: medullary thyroid carcinoma + pheochromocytoma + parathyroid hyperplasia
  • Primary hyperparathyroidism- clinical picture
  • Bone Disease: Osteitis fibrosa cystica - bone pain, bone deformities, pathologic fractures
  • Osteoporosis (with preferential loss of cortical bone)
  • Kidney Disease: Kidney stones (usually calcium oxalate stones)
  • Nephrocalcinosis: deposition of calcium in the renal medulla
  • Renal impairment: eGFR <60 mL/min.
  • Polydipsia, polyuria (chronic hypercalcemia->compromised renal concentrating ability).
  • CNS effects: lethargy, memory deficits, depression, psychosis, ataxia, stupor, coma.
  • Neuromuscular effects: weakness, proximal myopathy, hypertonia.
  • Cardiovascular effects: hypertension, bradycardia (and eventually asystole), ↓ QT interval.
  • Digestive effects: nausea, indigestion, vomiting, anorexia, constipation/ileus (hypercalcemia
  • ->↓ bowel motility), peptic ulcers, pancreatitis.
  • Eye findings: band keratopathy.
  • Systemic metastatic calcification: skin → itch; joints → chondrocalcinosis, eyes-> red eye sdr.

Primary hyperparathyroidism- diagnostic workup #2

  • 1. Blood tests:
  • Serum Ca: ↑ ionized (> 5 mg/dl)/ total Ca (> 10,5 mg/dl) !! The diagnosis of primary
  • Serum P: ↓ (<3.5 mg/dl) hyperparathyroidism is merely
  • Urinary Ca: ↑ (> 300 mg/24 h); Urinary P: ↑ (> 3 g/24h) biochemical: ↑ Ca + ↑ PTH
  • ALP: ↑ (> 60 U/L)- high bone turnover
  • 1,25(OH) D3: ↑ (> 76 ng/ml)
  • PTH: ↑ (> 60 pg/ml)- clearly inappropriate in a hypercalcemic patient
  • 2. Localization studies of abnormal parathyroid glands:
  • - part of the preoperative assessment
  • - options: - 99mTc-sestamibi scanning coupled with SPECT/CT- the most reliable
  • - Computed tomography/ Magnetic resonance imaging
  • - Ultrasound.
  • 3. Determining the presence of end-organ damage from hypercalcemia
  •  X-rays (lateral thoracolumbar spine, hands, and skull): vertebral compression fractures,
  • subperiosteal resorption (e.g. classic subperiosteal resorption of cortical bone of
  • phalanges), “salt and paper” appearance of the skull, bone cysts- in the central
  • medullary portions of the shafts of the metacarpals, ribs or pelvis, “brown tumors” – in
  • the trabecular portions of the jaw, the long bones and ribs, pathologic fractures.
  •  DXA (dual X-ray absorptiometry) - measurement of BMD-> osteoporosis.
  •  Renal function tests
  •  Renal imaging (urography, ultrasound, CT scan)- renal stones/nephrocalcinosis
  •  Dental films - loss of the lamina dura of the teeth.
  • Primary hyperparathyroidism- surgical treatment
  • Parathyroidectomy is indicated for all patients with symptomatic hyperparathyroidism, but
  • also for the asymptomatic patients who fulfill one of the following criteria:
  • • An increase in serum calcium>1 mg/dL above the upper limit of normal;
  • • An episode of severe hypercalcemia (>14 mg/dl) in the past history;
  • • Impaired renal function (eGFR < 60 ml/min);
  • • Renal stones (symptomatic or on radiograph);
  • • Urinary calcium excretion > 400 mg/24 h;
  • • Parathyroid bone disease, especially osteitis fibrosa cystica; BMD DXA T-score <−2.5 SD;
  • presence of vertebral fractures;
  • • Age< 50 years;

Primary hyperparathyroidism- surgical treatment #3

  • Parathyroidectomy= the definitive treatment of primary hyperparathyroidism
  • - Single parathyroid adenoma -> unilateral exploration (minimally invasive surgery) of
  • the neck with the removal of the single abnormal gland.
  • - Hyperplasia -> partial parathyroidectomy (3½-gland parathyroidectomy), perhaps
  • with reimplantation of tissue in a more accessible site- e.g. forearm
  • - After parathyroidectomy, a transitory postoperative hypocalcemia may appear
  • (functional inhibition of the remnant parathyroid glands and “hungry bone
  • syndrome” = uptake of Ca and P by the bones)→ replacement treatment with
  • calcium + vitamin D metabolites is needed, with progressive decrease of the doses
  • Primary hyperparathyroidism- medical treatment
  • !! There is no definitive medical therapy for primary hyperparathyroidism.
  • Options:
  •  Selective estrogen receptor modulator Do not have significant/ persistent effects
  • (SERM)-Raloxifene on serum calcium or intact PTH levels.
  •  Bisphosphonates- Alendronate etc.
  •  Calcimimetic agents- Cinacalcet -> may offer an alternative to surgery (in case surgery is
  • contraindicated/ refused by the patient/ it has failed to cure the hyperparathyroidism)
  • Acute hypercalcemia management:
  •  NaCl 0,9% 2-4 l/day IV + Furosemide 20-40 mg/day IV
  •  Calcitonin 4-8 UI/kg SC/ IM (effective only for 48 h due to tachyphylaxis)
  •  Bisphosphonates (Pamidronate, Zoledronate)
  •  +/- Dialysis
  • Hypocalcemia- causes
  •  Hypoparathyroidism
  •  Resistance to PTH action—Pseudohypoparathyroidism (PHP)
  •  Failure to produce 1,25(OH) D normally
  • • Vitamin D deficiency
  • • Hereditary vitamin D-dependent rickets, type 1 (alpha-hydroxylase deficiency)
  •  Resistance to 1,25(OH) D action
  • • Hereditary vitamin D-resistant rickets, type 2 (defective vitamin D receptor)
  •  Acute hypocalcemia (acute complexation or deposition of calcium)
  • • Acute hyperphosphatemia (rhabdomyolysis, rapid tumor lysis)
  • • Rapid, excessive skeletal mineralization (hungry bones syndrome, osteoblastic
  • metastasis)
  • Hypoparathyroidism- causes

 Surgical #4

  •  Autoimmune->may be associated with primary adrenal insufficiency and
  • mucocutaneous candidiasis (Type I polyglandular autoimmune syndrome).
  •  DiGeorge syndrome—congenital absence of the parathyroids, thymic aplasia,
  • immunodeficiency, and cardiac anomalies
  •  Radioactive iodine therapy for Graves’ disease
  •  Infiltrative: hemochromatosis, Wilson’s disease
  •  Idiopathic
  • Hypoparathyroidism- clinical picture
  • 1. Neuromuscular excitability
  •  Tingling, numbness (especially of fingers, toes, or lips), muscles cramps.
  •  Carpopedal spasm (the classic muscular component of tetany), trismus.
  •  Stridor (due to laryngospasm).
  •  Focal or generalized seizures (that can be resistant to classic antiepileptic agents, but
  • respond to normalization of serum calcium levels); confusion.
  • Lesser degrees of neuromuscular excitability produce latent tetany elicited by testing:
  • Chvostek sign: tapping the facial nerve about 2 cm anterior to the earlobe, just below the
  • zygoma-> twitching of the corner of the mouth.
  • Trousseau sign: inflating a blood pressure cuff to about 20 mmHg above systolic pressure for 3
  • min-> carpal spasm.
  • Weiss sign: tapping the facial nerve just anterior to the external auditory meatus-> twitching
  • of the corner of the eye.
  • 2. Other manifestations:
  •  Hyperirritability, anxiety, depression, shortness of breath.
  •  Cardiac effects : prolongation of QT intervals.
  •  Ophthalmologic effects : subcapsular cataract.
  •  Dermatologic effects : dry skin, coarse hair, brittle nails.
  •  In children: dental and enamel hypoplasia (if hypocalcemia is present during the
  • development of permanent teeth).
  •  Extrapyramidal signs (due to calcifications of basal ganglia)
  • Hypoparathyroidism- diagnostic workup

1. Blood tests: #5

  • Serum Ca: ↓ ionized (< 3,5 mg/dl)/ total Ca (<8.5 mg/dl)
  • Serum P: ↑ (>4.2 mg/dl)
  • Urinary Ca: ↓ (< 100 mg/24 h); Urinary P: ↓ (< 1 g/24h)
  • PTH: ↓ (< 20 pg/ml)
  • 2. ECG: prolongation of QT interval
  • 3. Electromyography- repetitive motor neuron action potentials, usually grouped as
  • doublets.
  • 4. Ophthalmology exam: subcapsular cataract
  • Hypoparathyroidism- treatment
  • Standard treatment options for hypoparathyroidism:
  • • Calcium supplements, orally—1–3 g of elemental calcium/day in divided doses.
  • • Activated vitamin D metabolites: – 1 α-calcidol (ALPHA-D3): 1–4 μg/day
  • – 1,25(OH)2vitD3 (calcitriol) (ROCALTROL): 1–3 μg/day
  • • An adequate vitamin D status: vitamin D supplementations in a daily dose of 400–800 IU.
  • !!The target serum calcium should be at the low end of the reference range-> to avoid
  • nephrocalcinosis and renal stones (the renal retention of calcium brought about by PTH is lost)
  • Acute hypocalcemia management =medical emergency (can cause laryngospasm and
  • seizures)
  • • Calcium gluconate 10% by slow IV infusion.
  • • Diazepam, anxiolytics.
  • • Rebreathing into a paper bag.
  • • Oral calcium and a rapidly acting preparation of vitamin D (e.g., calcitriol) should be started.
  • Osteoporosis- causes

Primary osteoporosis-> in postmenopausal women/ in older men due to age-related factors. #6

  • Secondary osteoporosis-> due to specific clinical disorders:
  • 1) Endocrine disorders:
  • 3) Gastrointestinal/nutrition disorders
  • - Hypogonadism
  • -Malabsorption syndromes: celiac sprue,
  • - Hyperprolactinemia
  • intestinal bypass, chronic pancreatitis
  • - Hyperparathyroidism
  • - Crohn’s disease
  • - Cushing syndrome
  • - Obstructive jaundice, biliary cirrhosis
  • - Hyperthyroidism
  • 4) Hematologic disorders :
  • - GH deficiency or IGF-1 deficiency
  • Multiple myeloma, systemic mastocytosis,
  • - Insulin dependent diabetes mellitus
  • leukemia
  • 2) Medications
  • 5) Collagen metabolism disorders
  • Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH)
  • Osteogenesis imperfecta
  • agonists, cyclosporine, glucocorticoids
  • Osteoporosis- clinical picture
  •  Usually clinically silent until an acute fracture occurs
  •  Typical vertebral fractures: sudden episode of well-localized pain that may initially
  • require bed rest but gradually subsides over 4–8 weeks; following vertebral fractures, a
  • patient may be left with persistent back pain, kyphosis, hyperlordosis, height loss (>4
  • cm)
  •  Peripheral fractures after low trauma (distal radius, humerus, hip)
  • Osteoporosis- investigations
  • Laboratory studies (employed to exclude Biochemical markers of bone turnover
  • secondary osteoporosis) (NOT routinely measured)
  •  Bone formation : alkaline
  • - ESR, FBC phosphatase (total/bone specific),
  • - serum calcium, phosphate osteocalcin
  • - urea, creatinine  Bone resorption : deoxypyridinoline,
  • - ASAT, ALAT, GGT C terminal telopeptide of type 1
  • - serum protein electrophoresis collagen, N terminal telopeptide of
  • - PTH, 25-OH vitamin D, TSH, FT4, urinary type 1 collagen
  • free cortisol, testosterone+ gonadotropin levels
  • (FSH, LH) Lateral thoracic and lumbar spine X-rays:
  • for detecting vertebral fractures and for
  • their follow-up
  • Osteoporosis- DXA (dual-energy X-ray
  • absorptiometry)

- For measurement of bone mineral density, usually carried out at the level of the hip and #7

  • lumbar spine; considered the gold standard for the diagnosis of osteoporosis.
  • - Bone mass is quoted in terms of the number of SD from an expected mean.
  • - A reduction of one SD in bone density will approximately double the risk of fracture.
  • T-score: number of SD patient’s BMD above or T score:
  • below average BMD of young–adult reference >−1 SD-> Normal
  • population- for postmenopausal women and men <−1 but ≥−2.5 SD-> Low bone mass (osteopenia)
  • >50 years old <−2.5 SD- Osteoporosis
  • Z-score: number of SD patient’s BMD above or <−2.5 SD+ fragility fracture- Established
  • below average BMD of age and gender-matched (severe) osteoporosis
  • reference population- children, young adults,
  • premenopausal women, men <50 years old
  • - FRAX score= a diagnostic tool that integrates clinical risk factors (age, fragility fractures,
  • hip fracture after 50 years in a first grade relative, weight< 57 kg, smoking, rheumatoid
  • arthritis, glucocorticoid therapy) and BMD at the femoral neck to calculate the 10-year
  • probability of hip fracture and the 10-year probability of a major osteoporotic fracture.
  • DXA- indications
  • - All women >65 years old and men >70 years old
  • - Women< 65 years old/ men< 70 years old with the following risk factors: current
  • cigarette smoker, loss of height, thoracic kyphosis
  • - Women< 65 years old at risk for osteoporosis: estrogen deficiency, history of maternal
  • hip fracture before the age of 50, BMI< 19 kg/m2, history of amenorrhea more than 1
  • years before the age of 42
  • - Glucocorticoid therapy equivalent to ≥ 5mg of prednisone/day, ≥3 months;
  • - Individuals with bone mass osteopenia or fragility fractures on imaging studies;
  • - Individuals >50 years old who develop wrist, hip, spine, or proximal humerus fracture
  • with minimal or no trauma, excluding pathologic fractures;
  • - Individuals with medical conditions that can cause secondary osteoporosis.
  • Osteoporosis- management
  • 1) Lifestyle changes
  • •Adjusting the home environment and reviewing the need for medications, such as hypnotics
  • and antihypertensives, for instance.
  • •Weight-bearing exercise (e.g., walking outdoors for 20 min 3× weekly)
  • •Well-balanced diet
  • • Adequate intake of Ca (≈1000–1200 mg/day), vitamin D and proteins
  • 2) Pharmacologic agents

ANTIRESORPTIVES: #8

  • a) Bisphosphonates (Alendronate, Risedronate, Zoledronic and Ibandronic acid)
  •  Available as PO/ IV administration depending on the type of bisphosphonate
  •  Oral bisphosphonates should be taken on an empty stomach, and 30–60 min
  • (depending on the drug) should pass prior to additional oral intake.
  •  Side effects: GI disturbance (nausea and esophagitis), osteonecrosis of the jaw
  • b) Calcitonin, SERM (Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulators), Hormone replacement
  • therapy (estrogen)
  • c) Denosumab (Prolia)= monoclonal antibody directed against RANKL
  • OSTEO-ANABOLIC (BONE-FORMING) AGENTS:
  • a) Recombinant human PTH (1–34) (Teriparatide): given in daily subcutaneous
  • doses has been shown to increase BMD and reduce fracture risk
  • b) Strontium ranelate
  • SPECT/CT- parathyroid adenoma
